summary: Welcome to Chaco Space Guard, an educational web game that connects space exploration with Chaco’s identity. The game invites players to learn science through three activities: identifying phenomena, exploring the region, and building a conceptual spacecraft. You can become an astronaut and lead a space mission to collect data on a meteor shower near the Moon. Or you can choose to be a scientist, managing the ground station in Campo del Cielo and learning scientific concepts as you complete tasks. The project uses data provided by NASA to create an interactive game, while also teaching players about the different roles in a space mission and the purpose of the tasks involved. It is suitable for anyone interested in learning more.
details:
What is Chaco Space Guard about?

Chaco Space Guard is an educational game designed to make space science accessible to everyone in a fun and straightforward way, connecting the game’s activities with NASA’s public educational resources.

In this game, you can choose between two important roles in a NASA research mission. Decide whether you want to carry out the tasks of an astronaut traveling through space or those of a scientist at a research base on Earth.

Ground station mission

During this stage, you’ll learn scientific concepts through three missions:

In “Alert at Campo del Cielo,” you’ll learn to identify astronomical phenomena. In “Cosmic Footprints,” you’ll explore the Chaco region and learn about Campo del Cielo, where a meteor shower occurred more than 4,000 years ago. Today, the area is home to the Pigüen N'onaxá Natural and Cultural Reserve. In “Sentinel Project,” you’ll build a satellite by choosing different modules, then send it into space to collect information.

Space travel mission

In this mission, you take on the role of an astronaut and plan and carry out a space journey. You’ll build a spacecraft within mass, budget, and energy limits, plan a flight path, and launch it to photograph different asteroids, gather information, and return safely to the ground station.

Objectives

To make scientific concepts easier to learn through an interactive, visual experience for all users, using NASA’s public educational resources.

Tools used

HTML, JavaScript, CSS

Data used

Meteors & Meteorites Facts — This resource helps players learn and distinguish key concepts. It also links to the original resource so they can continue learning. Its definitions support the classification activity: a meteoroid is a rock in space; a meteor is the luminous phenomenon in the atmosphere; and a meteorite is the fragment that reaches the ground.

We adapted these concepts into an interactive activity: players select a word and place it in the corresponding area of the scene. The resource provides the scientific explanations behind the answers.

NASA Worldview — This resource connects map exploration with satellite observation of the region. After learning about Quitilipi and Campo del Cielo, players can select “Explore resources” and open Worldview to compare the area.

The game’s interactive map is an original recreation. Satellite imagery is viewed outside the game in Worldview; it is not embedded in the scene. The mission is completed by exploring both locations.

Build It Yourself: NASA Webb — This resource teaches how scientific objectives guide the design of a space mission. We included it as a conceptual complement to the Sentinel-01 builder.

Our activity is simple, but it lets players install five modules and learn what each one does: a camera to capture images, a spectrometer to analyze materials using light, an antenna to transmit data, propulsion to perform maneuvers, and solar panels to generate electricity. The builder is original and does not reproduce the Webb telescope or its specifications.

Next Five Asteroid Approaches — This resource is used alongside Small-Body Database Lookup to identify the selected asteroid during the flight. This triggers an alert showing its distance and speed. Photographing the asteroid earns the player more points. These data provide scientific context, while the flight itself is a simulation.
